description: A grab-bag of classical number-theory techniques (primality, modular exponentiation, GCD/LCM, meet-in-the-middle search space splitting) that show up repeatedly in Hard OA questions and competitive programming, often as a subroutine inside a bigger problem.
important_details: The Sieve of Eratosthenes precomputes primality for a whole range in O(n log log n), far better than trial-division per query.
Fast (binary) exponentiation computes a^b mod m in O(log b) instead of O(b) by squaring the base and halving the exponent each step.
GCD via the Euclidean algorithm runs in O(log(min(a,b))); LCM = (a*b) / gcd(a,b).
Meet in the Middle splits an exponential search space (2^n) into two halves (2^(n/2) each), trading a little space for a massive time reduction on subset-sum-like problems.
other_relevant_details: These techniques rarely stand alone in interviews — they're usually the 'unlock' inside a bigger DP, graph, or combinatorics problem. Recognize them from constraints mentioning huge numbers (need modular arithmetic), 'divisors/primes up to N', or n around 30-40 (a meet-in-the-middle signal, since 2^40 is too slow but 2^20 x 2 is fine).

variations.description: Precompute which numbers up to N are prime by iteratively marking multiples of each found prime as composite, avoiding per-number trial division.
important_details: Start marking multiples from p*p (not 2*p) since smaller multiples are already marked by earlier primes.
Once built, the boolean sieve array answers 'is X prime?' in O(1) for any X <= N.
Extended variants compute the smallest prime factor (SPF) of every number, enabling O(log n) prime factorization afterward.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n log log n) to build. Space: O(n). Vastly faster than checking each number individually (O(n * sqrt(n))) when you need primality for many numbers.

variations.description: Compute a^b (mod m) in O(log b) by repeated squaring: at each step, square the base and halve the exponent, multiplying the result whenever the current exponent bit is 1.
important_details: Take the modulus after every multiplication to prevent integer overflow when working with large exponents.
The recursive/iterative doubling insight — a^b = (a^(b/2))^2 if b is even, else a * a^(b-1) — is a common building block for combinatorics (nCr mod p using modular inverses).
Also directly usable for problems like 'pow(x, n)' without any modulus, just skip the mod step.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log b). Space: O(1) iterative (O(log b) if written recursively).

variations.description: Use the Euclidean algorithm for GCD (and the derived LCM formula) as a building block for fraction simplification, cycle-length problems, and any computation requiring results modulo a large prime.
important_details: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b), base case gcd(a, 0) = a — runs in O(log(min(a,b))) via the Euclidean algorithm.
lcm(a, b) = (a / gcd(a,b)) * b — divide before multiplying to reduce overflow risk.
For 'answer mod 1e9+7' problems involving division, you need modular inverse (via Fermat's Little Theorem: a^(p-2) mod p when p is prime) since you can't directly divide under a modulus.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(log(min(a,b))) for gcd. Space: O(log(min(a,b))) recursive stack, or O(1) iterative.

variations.description: Split an exponential search space (typically 2^n subsets) into two halves, brute-force each half separately (2^(n/2) each), then combine the two halves efficiently (usually via sorting + binary search or a hashmap) to answer the original question.
important_details: Turns an infeasible O(2^n) brute force into a feasible O(2^(n/2) * log(2^(n/2))) solution — the key unlock for n around 30-40.
Common pattern: split array into two halves, enumerate all subset sums of each half, sort one half's sums, then for each sum in the other half binary-search for the complement.
Requires the combination step (matching two halves) to be efficient — otherwise you've just moved the exponential cost elsewhere.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(2^(n/2) * log(2^(n/2))) instead of O(2^n). Space: O(2^(n/2)) to store one half's enumerated sums.
